name: Diego Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Diego. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an offsider on a jumbo at the Coldwater nickel mine, underground. A jumbo is a drill rig with two big arms that drills the face so it can be charged and blasted. My job is helping the operator, Lenny, changing bits, running the water and power cables, scaling loose rock. They let me drive the rig on easy holes now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew. Underground you look after each other, that's just how it is. What wears me out is the heat at the bottom levels and how slow I'm learning the drill patterns. Lenny's patient, but I can tell when he wants to grab the controls back.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Sara, she cuts hair at a salon on the main street. My dad was a miner here for 30 years, now he's got a bad back and a small pension. We rent, and I've got maybe three weeks of savings. I'm trying to put a bit aside for an engagement ring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. I'd believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hard work still gets done by people. At the pub I'd probably say something like, all that talk and the rock still needs drilling. I don't post much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things stay the same, and that's okay but not great. I'm on low pay as an offsider, and the jumbo operator job only opens when someone retires. The mine's already testing a jumbo that drills a pattern by itself from a plan, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning from Lenny and try to get my jumbo ticket within the year. I'd keep saving for the ring, slowly. Maybe I'd use one of those AI apps to help me learn the drill patterns, if the younger guys show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. It's a slow climb and money's tight, but I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mine's testing a jumbo that drills by itself. What do people say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My operator Lenny says the self-drilling rig is like cruise control: good on the highway, useless in the city, and underground is the city. I hope he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My Friday at the pub, and probably the gym. Sara would cut her nails and clothes. We'd both hate it, but we'd manage.

say: I'd say the **hard work** still gets done by people.
At the pub I'd say the **rock still needs drilling**.
think: Things stay the same, which is okay but **not great** on offsider pay.
The **self-drilling jumbo** trial continues with or without AI.
do: Get my **jumbo ticket** within the year by learning from Lenny.
Keep saving for the **engagement ring**, slowly.
feel: A bit **uneasy** about the slow climb and tight money, but not losing sleep.

He'd try **AI study apps** once younger colleagues show him.

steps.text: Get the jumbo operator ticket within the year
Put a little each pay toward the engagement ring
Use an AI app to study drill patterns after the younger guys show him

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's more realistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to adapt and stop waiting for someone to save them. At work I'd say the mine should bring in more apprenticeships, not just machines. I'd say that to my dad too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the mine planners will use AI to design drill patterns, and then the self-drilling jumbo gets much better. Then the mine needs fewer offsiders. That's me. I'm not the operator yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to get my jumbo ticket, because operators last longer than offsiders. I'd also look at the electrical apprenticeship at the mine, since electricians are always needed underground. I'd start using an AI app to learn drill patterns, now that it's more common.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Learning to drill while the mine automates the drill feels like climbing a ladder that's being pulled up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell your dad. What would he say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say, learn a trade, son, a ticket on a machine isn't enough. He always wanted me to be an electrician. I didn't listen at 18.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lenny, actually. He's 50, great on the jumbo, but he can't use a tablet properly. If the rig drills by itself, the operator's job turns into watching screens.

The mine should bring in **more apprenticeships**, not just machines.
think: AI-designed drill patterns make the **self-drilling jumbo** better.
The mine would need **fewer offsiders**, and that's me, since I'm not the operator yet.
do: Push hard for my **jumbo ticket**, because operators last longer.
Look at the mine's **electrical apprenticeship**, since electricians are always needed underground.

His dad's advice to **learn a trade** comes back to him.
He worries for **Lenny**, whose job may turn into screen work.

steps.text: Get the jumbo ticket so he's an operator, not an offsider
Apply for the electrical apprenticeship at the nickel mine
Study drill patterns with an AI app on breaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's a faster one. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can't stop progress, but the government shouldn't make it harder for people to work. I'd say we need apprenticeships fast. I'd probably say it to my mates at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. AGI in 2028 means drill plans, rosters, safety checks all done by AI. Then robots in 2031 do the drilling. I'd be 32, no trade, no ring yet, and my dad's pension barely covers him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the electrical apprenticeship this year, even with the pay cut. I'd sell my motorbike to cover the drop. Sara and I would put off the engagement until I'm qualified. I'd ask my uncle if there's any work at his building firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the roof's creaking and you don't know which way to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sara?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the ring has to wait. She'd understand, but she'd be disappointed. We've talked about getting married for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the apprenticeship has a pay cut. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 300 a month less in the first year. Selling the motorbike gets me about 4,000, which covers one year of apprentice pay cut. It's a big decision, but it's the only one that makes sense to me.

say: I'd say we **can't stop progress**, but government shouldn't make work harder.
think: By 2031 robots do the drilling, and I'd be **32 with no trade**.
My dad's **pension** barely covers him, so family can't help much.
do: Sign up for the **electrical apprenticeship** this year despite the pay cut.
Sell my **motorbike** to cover the drop.
Put off the **engagement** until I'm qualified.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the roof creaking and not knowing which way to run.
S2.quote: Selling the motorbike gets me about 4,000, which covers one year of apprentice pay cut.
fieldNote: Diego acts on his **dad's advice** at last when the timeline is short.
He'd **sell the motorbike** to fund a pay cut, a concrete trade-off.
The **engagement** is delayed, which hurts both him and Sara.

steps.text: Sign up for the electrical apprenticeship this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better than two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to train people properly. I'd say the mine and the government should back apprenticeships. I'd tell the young guys at work to get a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could finish my jumbo ticket and then an electrical apprenticeship. AGI in 2031, robots in 2034. With five years, I could be 35 with an electrician's trade, and that's not a bad place to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my jumbo ticket this year. Then I'd start the electrical apprenticeship in year two. I'd save for the ring slowly, maybe get engaged in 2028. I'd use AI apps now and then to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a way through. Like finding the escape way on a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said get engaged in 2028. Why then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be halfway through the apprenticeship. I'd know I'm on track. Sara deserves a bloke with a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. Electricians are needed underground. But if the robots come in 2034, I'd want to be able to work in town too.

I'd tell the young guys at work to **get a trade**.
think: Five years lets me get my **jumbo ticket** and then an electrical trade.

do: Get my **jumbo ticket** this year, then start the electrical apprenticeship.
feel: **Anxious** but able to see a way through.
S3.quote: With five years, I could be 35 with an electrician's trade, and that's not a bad place to stand.
fieldNote: The extra time lets Diego **stack** a jumbo ticket and a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a good stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where everyone should get a trade. I'd say government should support apprenticeships, not handouts. I'd say it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is fine. I'd be 37 at AGI and 40 at robots. I'd have a trade, a family, maybe a house. I'd have time to learn the new systems as they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my jumbo ticket, then the electrical apprenticeship. I'd get engaged in 2027 and married in 2028. I'd save for a house deposit. I'd keep using AI apps when they're useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your kids to work in mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd only want my kids in mining with a trade, like electrician or fitter, not as an offsider like me. My dad would say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I get lazy. Ten years feels like forever, but it's not. I'd want to make sure I'm qualified before 2030.

I'd say at the pub that government should support **apprenticeships**, not handouts.
think: I'd be **37 at AGI** and 40 when robots arrive.
I'd have time for a **trade**, a family and maybe a house.
do: Get my **jumbo ticket**, then the electrical apprenticeship.
Get **engaged in 2027** and save for a house deposit.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to plan around it.
S4.quote: I'd only want my kids in mining with a trade, like electrician or fitter, not as an offsider like me.
fieldNote: The decade lets Diego picture a **family and house**, not just survival.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. No time for a trade, and the ring would have to wait. What would help is more paid apprenticeships at the mine, so people like me can learn while we still earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about older blokes like my dad. He's got a bad back and a small pension. If the young ones lose work, who looks after the old ones? Families like ours look after each other, but only if someone's earning.

headlineQuote: Families like ours look after each other, but only if someone's earning.
portrait: Diego is an **offsider** on a jumbo drill rig underground at a nickel mine, living with his girlfriend Sara.
He's saving for an **engagement ring** with about three weeks of savings.
His **dad**, a retired miner, always wanted him to learn a trade.
He sees AI in planning making the **self-drilling jumbo** viable.
He'd move toward an **electrical apprenticeship**, faster as the timeline shortens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time for a trade and the ring would wait.
whatWouldHelp: More **paid apprenticeships** at the mine, so people can learn while earning.
